newsitem.title: USA: Miami did not disclose deficit in bond documents.
newsitem.headline: Miami did not disclose deficit in bond documents.

text.p: Miami did not disclose its worsening financial condition in documents for any of the four bond and notes issues it did last year, officials and sources who worked on the deals said Tuesday.
It was unclear which city officials knew about the growing deficit, now estimated at $68 million for fiscal year 1997, which began October 1.
City comissioners said they were unaware of the budget gap until a few weeks ago.
While many of those who worked on the deals were unavailable or declined to comment, others said they also were unaware of the deficit.

"They represented to us that their position was fine and that there was nothing of a material nature that they needed to disclose," said Percy Aguila, a vice president at Rauscher Pierce Refsnes Inc, which was senior manager for the city's $72 million special obligation bond issue for pensions in December 1995.
"If we were aware of it, not only would we have disclosed it, it would have been all over the official statement," Aguila said.
"We were kind of victims of the same lack of forthrightness that the City Commission was," said Mike Abrams, a first vice president at Rauscher.
The Securities and Exchange Commission's regional director, Charles Senatore, declined to comment on any disclosure concerns, if any, the agency might have about Miami bonds.
New disclosure rules for the municipal market require that most bond issuers provide timely information on their fiscal conditions.

To that end, the SEC has stepped up its efforts to insure issurers comply with the news riules. Last week, the SEC charged that Arizona's Maricopa County violated the anti-fraud provisions of federal securities laws by failing to disclose in a pair of 1993 bond issues that its financial condition had deteriorated since its last financial statements were issued.
The SEC said Maricopa also failed to disclose that it used some of the bond proceeds to ease its cash flow deficit, instead for the projects outlined in the bond documents.
Maricopa settled the charges last week by agreeing to cease and desist from current and future violations, but did not admit guilt or pay a fine.
City of Miami officials have already confirmed that the SEC is investigating the pension bond issue, which was insured by AMBAC Indemnity Corp, a unit of AMBAC Inc.
In that case, the bond documents clearly said $25 million of the proceeds would be used to reimburse the general fund for the current year's pension fund contribution.
The issue was validated in court, and no appeals were raised.
But at the very least, said acting Miami City Manager Merrett Stierheim, the issue should have raised some eyebrows about the city's situation because debt was used for basic operating expenses.
"Wasn't that bond issue an indication of fiscal decay?" Stierheim said during an emergency budget meeting Monday.

Stierheim and Commissioner J.L. Plummer sought assurances at that meeting that the proceeds of a $21 million revenue bond issue in October, 1995, had not been used to inflate the city's general fund balance.

City auditors assured them the bond proceeds were carried on the books as "restricted funds" until they were used for their intended purpose, the purchase of an office building and related moving costs.
The city also issued $20 million of general obligation bonds for sewers in June, 1995, and $20 million of tax anticipation notes in October 1995. It has not issued any debt in 1996."
--Jane Sutton, 305-374-5013
